catalog_quote: (5) Summary of metrical parameters a. The final syllable is extrametrical, unless extrametricality would render the whole word invisible or unaccentable. b. Northern East Cree is quantity-sensitive at the level of the nucleus. A heavy (H) syllable contains an historically long vowel or a rising diphthong. A light (L) syllable contains an historically short vowel. c. There is no Weight-By-Position. d. Feet are iambic; footing is from the right edge of the word, excluding the final syllable. e. There are no degenerate (L) feet. f. End Rule Right: the rightmost metrical prominence is accented. ... (6) Extrametrical final syllable a. The final syllable is never accented. b. Either the penult or antepenult is accented. (5b): Evidence for quantity-sensitivity is provided in (7): Northern East Cree accents the penult if it is heavy; otherwise it accents the antepenult. ... audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation, the domain quotation and the exceptions quotation are all verbatim in the held Dyck, Brittain & MacKenzie 2006 text at the stated sections/pages. (2) The deciding source is a 2006 dedicated accent/metrical paper (CLA proceedings, 14 pp) by the MUN East Cree documentation team; it is the description every later work cites. Glottolog lists no phonology and its one 'grammar' (Collette 2014) is a morphology thesis; web search (CLA, CCLAS outputs, Algonquian Papers, TWPL, CJL, MUN/Laval/LAC repositories) found no reference grammar with a prosody chapter and no fuller instrumental study of accent placement. sources.citation: Davies, Katharine. 2020. An exploratory descriptive study of accent shift in Northern East Cree. Toronto Working Papers in Linguistics 42. 8 pp.
sources.quote: 'Each word in NE Cree contains one accented syllable, which correlates with a higher pitch, and to a lesser degree, intensity ... in the non-final accent pattern, words are accented on either the penultimate syllable or the antepenultimate syllable. When the penultimate syllable is long, accent falls on the penultimate syllable. When the antepenultimate vowel is long, and the penultimate vowel is short, accent falls on the long antepenultimate syllable. When both antepenultimate and penultimate vowels are short, the accent can fall on either syllable (MacKenzie 1980).' Final accent pattern wit

sources.citation: Dyck, Carrie, Alethea Power & Kevin Terry. 2012. Syncope in East Cree: Phonological or Phonetic? Papers of the 42nd Algonquian Conference (2010), 119-132. (plus CCLAS handout)
sources.quote: 'Syncope only affects syllables containing a short vowel (MacKenzie 1980) ... the location of syncope is predictable from foot structure; however foot structure is largely abstract, since there is only one pitch-accented vowel per word and hence only one "audible" foot (Dyck et al. 2006, 2008).' Confirms the single-accent domain and no secondary stress; silent on placement details.

sources.citation: Rose, Yvan & Julie Brittain. 2011. Grammar Matters: Evidence from Phonological and Morphological Development in Northern East Cree. In M. Pirvulescu et al. (eds.), Selected Proceedings of GALANA 4, 193-208. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla Proceedings Project (doc. #2596).
sources.quote: 'NE Cree words have one pitch accent per citation form. Accent falls on one of the last three syllables ... The final accent is morphologically conditioned [suffix -h voids final extrametricality] ... Non-final accent either falls on the penult or the antepenult ... the penult is accented when it is long; in contrast, the antepenult is accented when it is long and the penult is short. ... if both the penult and antepenult are short, the rules of accent placement are unclear ... accent in some words might be lexicalized ...
